questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: An individual is displaying rapid eye movement, suppressed muscle tone, and is difficult to wake up. When s/he does awake, s/he reports dreaming. The cycle of sleep s/he was experiencing is:
questions.explanation: REM sleep is characterized by rapid eye movements, muscle atonia (suppressed tone), high arousal threshold, and vivid dreaming.
questions.keyConcept: REM sleep is characterized by rapid eye movements, muscle atonia, and vivid dreaming.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: What seems to be the purpose of atonia during REM sleep?
options: It keeps the person or animal from suddenly waking up
It protects the brain from becoming too synchronized
It prevents the person or animal from acting out their dreams
questions.explanation: REM atonia is a paralysis of most skeletal muscles that prevents dream enactment (REM sleep behavior disorder occurs when this mechanism fails).
questions.keyConcept: REM atonia prevents dream enactment.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Which of the following is not true about night terrors?
options: Usually occur in the last third of sleep
Median age of onset is 6 years
questions.explanation: Night terrors occur during NREM deep sleep (stages 3–4), typically in the first third of the night, not the last third.
questions.keyConcept: Night terrors occur during NREM deep sleep in the first third of the night.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Maslow called the higher needs:
questions.explanation: Maslow distinguished lower deficiency needs (physiological, safety, belonging, esteem) from higher growth/being needs (self-actualization, transcendence).
questions.keyConcept: Maslow's higher needs are growth/being needs (self-actualization, transcendence).

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: The humanistic theory of personality proposed by Carl Rogers is called:
questions.explanation: Rogers developed client-centered (or person-centered) therapy, which emphasizes unconditional positive regard, empathy, and congruence.
questions.keyConcept: Rogers developed client-centered therapy emphasizing unconditional positive regard.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: According to Freud, the id is governed by the:
questions.explanation: The id operates on the pleasure principle, seeking immediate gratification of instincts and avoiding pain.
questions.keyConcept: The id operates on the pleasure principle, seeking immediate gratification.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: A defining characteristic of traits is that they are:
questions.explanation: Traits are stable, enduring patterns of behavior, thought, and emotion that persist across time and situations.
questions.keyConcept: Traits are stable, enduring patterns of behavior.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: The humanistic viewpoint emphasizes which of the following?
options: Determinism, the unconscious and biological drives
The idea that "the environment is the key causal matrix"
questions.explanation: Humanism focuses on conscious experience, free will, personal growth, and the drive toward self-actualization.
questions.keyConcept: Humanism focuses on free will, personal growth, and self-actualization.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Which of the following is an unconscious personality structure made up of the reality self, responsible for compromising and maintaining harmony?
questions.explanation: The ego mediates between the id’s impulses and the superego’s demands, operating on the reality principle to maintain balance.
questions.keyConcept: The ego mediates between id and superego, operating on reality principle.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Pavlov is famous for his work in:
questions.explanation: Pavlov’s experiments with dogs demonstrated that a neutral stimulus (bell) could come to elicit a salivation response after pairing with food – the foundation of classical conditioning.
questions.keyConcept: Pavlov discovered classical conditioning through salivation experiments.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: A bakery gives customers a free pastry after every 6 pastry purchases. This is an example of what kind of reinforcement schedule?
questions.explanation: Reinforcement occurs after a fixed number of responses (6 purchases) – that is a fixed-ratio schedule.
questions.keyConcept: Fixed-ratio schedule reinforces after a set number of responses.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: In classical conditioning, UR and CR are:
questions.explanation: The unconditioned response (UR) and conditioned response (CR) are typically the same or very similar behavior (e.g., salivation to food and to bell).
questions.keyConcept: UR and CR are typically the same or similar behavior.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Giving a student extra homework after they misbehave in class is an example of:
questions.explanation: Adding an aversive stimulus (extra homework) to decrease a behavior is positive punishment.
questions.keyConcept: Positive punishment adds an aversive stimulus to decrease behavior.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: After being bitten by a big dog, Ahmed was scared of other big dogs but he was not scared of little dogs. This pattern demonstrates:
questions.explanation: Ahmed discriminates between big dogs (feared) and little dogs (not feared), responding differently to similar but distinct stimuli.
questions.keyConcept: Discrimination is responding differently to distinct stimuli.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Positive reinforcement ______ the likelihood of a behaviour, and negative reinforcement ______ the likelihood of behaviour.
questions.explanation: Both positive reinforcement (adding a reward) and negative reinforcement (removing an aversive stimulus) increase the likelihood of a behavior.
questions.keyConcept: Both positive and negative reinforcement increase behavior likelihood.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Aggression always:
options: Is committed by someone who has been deliberately provoked
questions.explanation: The core definition of aggression is behavior intended to harm another person who wants to avoid that harm. Physical pain or emotional arousal is not required.
questions.keyConcept: Aggression is defined as behavior intended to harm another who wishes to avoid harm.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: In a revision of frustration‑aggression theory, Berkowitz theorized that:
options: Aggression cues can release bottled‑up anger
Frustration produces escape more often than aggression
Aggression is learned through a modeling effect
questions.explanation: Berkowitz added that environmental cues associated with aggression (e.g., weapons) can trigger aggressive responses when frustration has already created anger.
questions.keyConcept: Berkowitz added that environmental aggression cues can trigger responses.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: A person kicking a cat after losing a game of checkers is an example of:
questions.explanation: Displacing aggression from the real source of frustration (the opponent or the loss) onto a safer, less threatening target (the cat).
questions.keyConcept: Displacement redirects aggression from the source to a safer target.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Research has shown a positive correlation between aggression and the level of:
questions.explanation: Higher testosterone levels are associated with increased aggressive behavior in both animal and human studies.
questions.keyConcept: Higher testosterone levels correlate with increased aggression.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: How many types of aggression are there?
questions.explanation: The most common division is into hostile (affective, impulsive) aggression and instrumental (proactive, goal‑directed) aggression.
questions.keyConcept: Two main types: hostile and instrumental aggression.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: The leading researchers into SLT and aggression were by who?
questions.explanation: Albert Bandura’s social learning theory (Bobo doll experiment) demonstrated that aggression is learned through observation and modeling.
questions.keyConcept: Bandura's social learning theory demonstrated aggression through modeling.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Types of aggression:
questions.explanation: Hostile aggression is one of the two major types (along with instrumental aggression). The other options are not recognized categories.
questions.keyConcept: Hostile aggression is one of the two major types.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: ______ is the capacity for learning certain and specific abilities.
questions.explanation: Aptitude refers to the potential or capacity to learn specific skills or knowledge, whereas achievement measures what has already been learned.
questions.keyConcept: Aptitude is the potential to learn specific skills.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: IQ may be defined as:
options: Mental age (MA) x Chronological age (CA) x 100
questions.explanation: The traditional formula for IQ is (MA/CA) × 100, with 100 representing average performance.
questions.keyConcept: IQ = (MA/CA) × 100, with 100 as average.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: If a girl has an intelligence quotient of 100, we know that she has a:
options: Perfect score on a set of age‑related tests
Test performance superior to 90% of other children the same age
Mental age typical of children who have the same chronological age
Mental age below those of children with the same chronological age
questions.explanation: IQ of 100 means mental age equals chronological age – average for her age group.
questions.keyConcept: IQ of 100 indicates mental age equals chronological age.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: The Wechsler adult intelligence scale can be used to assess eligibility for:
questions.explanation: WAIS is used in clinical and educational settings to identify cognitive strengths/weaknesses, often for special educational support.
questions.keyConcept: WAIS identifies cognitive strengths/weaknesses for special educational support.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Kohlberg identified the three levels of moral development as the:
questions.explanation: Kohlberg’s three levels are: preconventional (self‑interest), conventional (social rules), and postconventional (abstract principles).
questions.keyConcept: Kohlberg's levels: preconventional (self), conventional (social), postconventional (principles).

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: A toddler learning to use the toilet who sometimes feels bad when he or she "messes up" is at Erikson's stage called:
questions.explanation: Erikson’s second stage (ages ~1–3) centers on developing independence; toilet training is a key task, and failure leads to shame/doubt.
questions.keyConcept: Autonomy vs. shame/doubt is Erikson's second stage (1-3 years).

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Which represents the correct order of Piaget's stages of intellectual development?
options: Sensorimotor, concrete operational, formal operational, post operational
Preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational, sensorimotor
Sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational
Preoperational, informal operational, formal operational, post operational
questions.explanation: Piaget’s correct sequence: sensorimotor (0–2), preoperational (2–7), concrete operational (7–11), formal operational (12+).
questions.keyConcept: Piaget's sequence: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: According to Jean Piaget’s cognitive development theory, the concrete operational stage is characterized by:
options: Grasping concepts of conservation of mass and understanding relations
Forming hypotheses and systematically testing them
Occurring in ages from 2 to 7 years old
questions.explanation: Concrete operational stage (ages 7–11) features conservation, logical thinking about concrete events, and understanding relationships.
questions.keyConcept: Concrete operational stage features conservation and logical thinking about concrete events.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: In moral development, conventional conformity means:
options: The individual behaves appropriately to avoid punishment
The individual behaves appropriately to avoid disapproval by others
The individual behaves appropriately to receive a reward
The individual behaves appropriately to respect rules and laws
questions.explanation: At the conventional level’s “good boy/good girl” orientation, behavior is driven by a desire to gain approval and avoid disapproval from others.
questions.keyConcept: Conventional conformity is driven by desire for approval and avoidance of disapproval.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Which of the following most clearly demonstrates the existence of emotional attachment?
questions.explanation: Separation anxiety (distress when separated from a primary caregiver) is a strong indicator of an emotional attachment bond.
questions.keyConcept: Separation anxiety is a strong indicator of emotional attachment.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: A child is largely nonverbal, is learning to coordinate purposeful movements with sense information, and is developing the concept of object permanence. The child is in Piaget’s stage:
questions.explanation: Sensorimotor stage (birth–2 years) includes development of object permanence, coordination of sensory input with motor actions, and pre‑language communication.
questions.keyConcept: Sensorimotor stage (0-2 years) includes object permanence and sensory-motor coordination.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Locus of control refers to:
options: The tendency for group decisions to be more extreme than individual decisions
The increase in obedience behaviour when encouraged by authority figures
Placing the onus of responsibility within or outside self
The characteristic of an authoritarian leader
questions.explanation: Locus of control is the degree to which people believe they have control over events (internal) versus outside forces (external).
questions.keyConcept: Locus of control is belief about control over events (internal vs. external).

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: In social psychology, conformity refers to which of the following:
options: Is the change that occurs in response to minority influence
A change in belief or behaviour in response to group pressure
Refers to change in behaviour in response to a command or order from an authority figure
Is evident in the phenomena of bystander effect
Is the result of group polarisation
questions.explanation: Conformity is adjusting one’s attitudes or actions to align with real or imagined group norms.
questions.keyConcept: Conformity is adjusting attitudes/actions to align with group norms.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: The psychology of attribution:
options: States that people over‑emphasise the personal influence to explain observed behaviour in others
Refers to a person's individual personality traits
Refers to the cognitive labelling theory which assigns causal explanations to observed events
Is related to the locus of control
Refers to the association between an event, person or feeling and the situation
questions.explanation: Attribution theory describes how people infer the causes of their own and others’ behavior (e.g., internal vs. external factors).
questions.keyConcept: Attribution theory describes how people infer causes of behavior.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: The drive‑theory of aggressive behaviour states that aggression results from:
options: Depiction of violence in the media
questions.explanation: Drive theory (frustration‑aggression hypothesis) proposes that frustration creates a drive to aggress; “poor frustration tolerance” is the closest match among options.
questions.keyConcept: Drive theory (frustration-aggression) proposes frustration creates drive to aggress.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Reasons of frustration include:
questions.explanation: Frustration arises from external barriers, internal conflicts, and personal limitations (skills, resources, etc.).
questions.keyConcept: Frustration arises from environmental obstacles, conflicts, and personal limitations.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: According to Freud, a process that distorts reality to prevent the individual from being overwhelmed by anxiety is known as:
questions.explanation: Defense mechanisms are unconscious strategies the ego uses to distort reality and reduce anxiety.
questions.keyConcept: Defense mechanisms are unconscious ego strategies to reduce anxiety.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: According to Freud, the defense mechanism that involves reverting to immature behaviors that have relieved anxiety in the past is:
questions.explanation: Regression is a return to earlier, less mature behaviors (e.g., tantrums, thumb‑sucking) when faced with stress.
questions.keyConcept: Regression is return to earlier, less mature behaviors under stress.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: In Freud's theory, the part of the personality that helps the individual adapt to external reality by making compromises between the id, the superego, and the environment is the:
questions.explanation: The ego operates on the reality principle, mediating between id impulses, superego demands, and external reality.
questions.keyConcept: The ego mediates between id, superego, and reality.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: The defense mechanism known as ______ involves attributing one's own undesirable feelings to other people.
questions.explanation: Projection is attributing one’s own unacceptable thoughts, feelings, or motives to someone else.
questions.keyConcept: Projection attributes one's own unacceptable feelings to others.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: "Everyone around me thinks they're big, funny and clever. They're all telling me my goldfish hiding Swimmy has died. They even thought I'd be fooled by flushing a pretend one down the toilet. She's only stiff because she's cold. But It's ok...I put boiling water in there so she could warm up." What defence mechanism does this show?
questions.explanation: The person refuses to accept the reality that the fish is dead (denying the painful truth).
questions.keyConcept: Denial is refusing to accept painful reality.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: "I'm sure my boyfriend has been cheating on me. When I find out he'll be sorry. Oh yeah and I need to buy my husband a birthday present..." What defence mechanism am I experiencing?
questions.explanation: The speaker refers to both a "boyfriend" and a "husband" – denying the reality of being married (or of infidelity) by contradictory statements.
questions.keyConcept: Denial involves contradictory statements that avoid reality.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: "It's so unfair! My mum doesn't care how much I cry and scream, she won't get me a car. She doesn't even care about me! She hates me!" What defence mechanism does this demonstrate?
questions.explanation: The person reverts to childlike emotional outbursts (crying, screaming, tantrums) – a return to earlier, less mature behavior.
questions.keyConcept: Regression reverts to childlike emotional outbursts.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: During an encounter judged as stressful, cortisol is released by the:
questions.explanation: Cortisol is secreted by the adrenal cortex as part of the HPA axis response to stress.
questions.keyConcept: Cortisol is secreted by adrenal cortex via HPA axis.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: The release of ______ decreases the effectiveness of the immune system in responding to prolonged stress.
questions.explanation: Chronic elevated corticosteroids (e.g., cortisol) suppress immune function, increasing susceptibility to illness.
questions.keyConcept: Chronic corticosteroids suppress immune function.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: At the time of acute stress, the adrenal medulla releases ______ that grows heart rate and respiration.
questions.explanation: The adrenal medulla secretes epinephrine and norepinephrine (catecholamines), which increase heart rate, respiration, and blood pressure.
questions.keyConcept: Adrenal medulla secretes catecholamines (epinephrine/norepinephrine) for fight-or-flight.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: According to the Cannon‑Bard theory of emotion:
options: Emotional experience and physiological arousal occur at the same time
questions.explanation: Cannon‑Bard proposes that the thalamus sends simultaneous signals to the cortex (emotion) and body (arousal).
questions.keyConcept: Cannon-Bard: simultaneous emotional and physiological responses.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: According to the James‑Lange theory of emotion:
options: Emotional experience and physiological arousal occur at the same time
questions.explanation: James‑Lange states that we feel emotion after our body reacts (e.g., “I feel afraid because I am trembling”).
questions.keyConcept: James-Lange: body reaction first, then emotion.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: According to Abraham Maslow:
options: Human behavior is directed by sex and aggression
Human beings start their development of motivation from the tip of hierarchy
A human being always can pass to higher level from the hierarchy without satisfaction of the lower level
Feeling safe and secure is one of the lower levels of hierarchy
Innovation and creation are present at the base of the hierarchy
questions.explanation: Safety needs are the second level (after physiological) in Maslow’s hierarchy – relatively low, but not the base.
questions.keyConcept: Safety needs are second level in Maslow's hierarchy.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Self‑actualization is:
options: A continuous state of success and achievement a human being can attain
A psychodynamic concept presented with Freud
Achieved at the base of hierarchy of needs
One of the important physiological needs
A concept introduced by Abraham Maslow
questions.explanation: Self‑actualization (fulfilling one’s potential) is the peak of Maslow’s hierarchy.
questions.keyConcept: Self-actualization is the peak of Maslow's hierarchy.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: In the development of language, the child by the age of 1–2 years:
questions.explanation: By 12–18 months, most children have a vocabulary of about 20–50 words; “25 words” is a reasonable average for that range.
questions.keyConcept: By 12-18 months, typical vocabulary is 20-50 words.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: The set of rules that governs the proper use and combination of language symbols is:
questions.explanation: Syntax refers to the grammatical rules for combining words into phrases and sentences.
questions.keyConcept: Syntax is grammatical rules for combining words.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Learning the speech sounds of the native language is known as:
questions.explanation: Phonology is the study of the sound system of a language, including phonemes and their patterns.
questions.keyConcept: Phonology is the study of a language's sound system.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Semantics refers to:
options: Knowledge of the rules of combining words in sentences
questions.explanation: Semantics is the branch of language concerned with meaning (words, phrases, sentences).
questions.keyConcept: Semantics concerns meaning in language.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Pragmatics is:
questions.explanation: Pragmatics covers the social use of language – context, inference, turn‑taking, politeness, etc.
questions.keyConcept: Pragmatics covers social use of language and context.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Syntax is:
options: Knowledge of how words and phrases can be combined
Subtle sound differences between similar words
questions.explanation: Syntax deals with sentence structure and the rules for combining words into grammatical sequences.
questions.keyConcept: Syntax deals with sentence structure and combination rules.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: The suggestion that infants are born as "universal language perceivers" according to Chomsky refers to:
options: An ability to distinguish between different languages
A preference for the native language over others
An inability to distinguish between different languages
An ability to discriminate between all sounds used in all languages
questions.explanation: Infants initially can perceive phonetic contrasts from any language; this ability narrows to their native language by about 12 months.
questions.keyConcept: Infants can initially discriminate all phonetic contrasts.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: The definition of memory is that it is an active system that receives, organizes, and:
questions.explanation: Memory involves three processes: encoding (receiving), storage (holding), and retrieval.
questions.keyConcept: Memory involves encoding, storage, and retrieval.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: The first step in placing information into memory storage is:
questions.explanation: Sensory memory (iconic/echoic) holds raw sensory input very briefly before further processing.
questions.keyConcept: Sensory memory holds raw input briefly before processing.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Procedural memory, unlike declarative memory, is responsible for:
questions.explanation: Procedural memory (implicit memory) stores how to perform skills and habits (“knowing how”).
questions.keyConcept: Procedural memory stores skills and habits ('knowing how').

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Why are mnemonic devices effective?
options: To remember material, you must first pay attention to it
Memory depends on the strategy of memory organization and how often it is rehearsed
questions.explanation: Mnemonics improve encoding by organizing information and providing retrieval cues, often through rehearsal.
questions.keyConcept: Mnemonics improve encoding through organization and rehearsal.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: The process of holding information in memory is referred to as:
questions.explanation: Storage is the retention of encoded information over time.
questions.keyConcept: Storage is retention of encoded information.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: The storage capacity of long‑term memory is best described as:
questions.explanation: Long‑term memory is considered to have virtually unlimited capacity; we never “fill it up.”
questions.keyConcept: Long-term memory has virtually unlimited capacity.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: The inability to recall events preceding an accident involving injuries to the head is called:
questions.explanation: Retrograde amnesia is loss of memory for events that occurred before the trauma or injury.
questions.keyConcept: Retrograde amnesia is loss of memory for events before trauma.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: According to the interference theory of forgetting:
options: Memory capacity is limited so that when new information is brought in, older memories must be removed
New learning can inhibit the retrieval of stored memory, and vice versa
Forgetting is directly related to the complexity and meaningfulness of the incoming information
Cues present at the time of learning interfere with memory retrieval
questions.explanation: Interference theory proposes that forgetting occurs because other information competes with retrieval (proactive and retroactive interference).
questions.keyConcept: Interference theory: other information competes with retrieval.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: An imaginary perception, such as seeing, hearing, or smelling something that does not exist in the external world is called a(n):
questions.explanation: A hallucination is a sensory perception without an external stimulus. (A delusion is a false belief.)
questions.keyConcept: Hallucination is sensory perception without external stimulus.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Television advertisements that are in black and white are just trying to take advantage of which attention getting technique?
questions.explanation: Black‑and‑white ads use contrast (light vs. dark, absence of color) to stand out and capture attention.
questions.keyConcept: Contrast (light/dark) captures attention.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: Illusions are:
questions.explanation: Illusions are misperceptions of real external stimuli (e.g., the Müller‑Lyer illusion), not creations from nothing.
questions.keyConcept: Illusions are misperceptions of real external stimuli.
